title: What Is a Generative AI Textbook and How Does It Compare to a Traditional Textbook?
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Meyer takes David Wiley's idea of a generative textbook, a set of crafted prompts a learner uses with a large language model, and actually tries it using an open calculus text's motivating questions in ChatGPT. He concludes that the generative version is currently worse on typography, layout and correctness, but says the more interesting question is whether it will improve. He then names shortcomings he cannot see technology resolving: a lack of distinctive voice, no editorial oversight on contested content, no cross-chapter coherence, and weakened bonds between students and teachers because every learner receives different problems. The move is to test an AI-in-education proposal against what a textbook actually does for learning instead of against its surface polish. The post also has a short links section on AI in education.
points: A hands-on trial shows the generative textbook is currently worse than a traditional one on typography, layout and correctness.
Probabilistic prose is competent but indistinct, and the best textbooks have a voice a model may not reproduce.
Without an author or editor, no one is accountable for contested or biased content, especially on state-specific history standards.
A traditional textbook builds on earlier chapters because its author remembers them, whereas a chat session has limited context across a semester.
Because each student gets different generated problems, they cannot compare notes and the teacher cannot review a shared hard problem.
quotes: Is the generative textbook better or worse than a traditional textbook right now?” isn’t all that interesting a question to me any more. I think it’s very hard to conduct an impartial analysis of the two options and conclude anything other than the generative textbook is right now worse than the traditional textbook in almost every way.

The more interesting question to me is, “Will the generative textbook be better or worse?” What will the generative textbook look like after a month of improvements to the generative model that created it?

I am not the first person to point out that generative AI produces prose that is competent but indistinct. This owes to the probabilistic way it constructs sentences and paragraphs. It’s cheerful and dull.

Which points of view will generative textbooks present? How can we hold these models, which researchers argue inherit the biases of their training data, accountable for ideas that are incorrect or dehumanizing to the kids who read them? Generative textbooks, by definition, lack an author or an editor, and many of the most popular generative AI models lack transparency into the ways they respond to these sensitive questions.

That useful pedagogical move is only possible because the author, Matthew Boelkins, knows what he wrote previously. When you start a chatGPT session in Week 5 of the semester, will your generative textbook remember what you learned in Week 1 of the semester and use it as a foundation for new learning?

This means that if I don’t understand problem #3, I can’t message a friend in class and ask, “Have you done #3 in the problem set yet? I have a question about it.” #3 is different in both of our problem sets. Moreover, the teacher can’t do what teachers often do when their students encounter the same difficult problem in a problem set: review it together.
